timeline.event: North American Rockwell's 1962 specification to Beech Aircraft called for the oxygen-tank heater assembly to run on the spacecraft's 28 V dc. A 1965 revision said the heaters should also run on a 65 V dc ground supply at KSC, to pressurize the tanks faster. Beech never changed the specification for the protective thermostatic switches, so they stayed rated for 28 V. NASA, North American Rockwell and Beech all missed this in their document reviews, and no test cycled the switches under load.
sources: Report of Apollo 13 Review Board (Cortright Report, 15 Jun 1970), ch.5 findings h-j, https://apollojournals.org/afj/ap13fj/pdf/report-of-a13-review-board-19700615-19700076776.pdf

timeline.event: At North American Rockwell (Downey), the oxygen shelf holding the future Apollo 13 tank no. 2 (serial 10024X-TA0008) was being removed from SM 106, the Apollo 10 service module. One retaining bolt had been left in place, the lifting fixture broke, and the shelf dropped about 2 inches (5 cm). The tank's closeout cap may have hit the shelf above. The Review Board judged it PROBABLE that this jarring loosened the fill tube. The shelf was later installed in SM 109 (Apollo 13) on 22 Nov 1968.
sources: Review Board report pp.4-20/4-21 and finding c, https://apollojournals.org/afj/ap13fj/pdf/report-of-a13-review-board-19700615-19700076776.pdf

timeline.event: The Countdown Demonstration Test began at KSC. Afterwards oxygen tank no. 2 would not empty by the normal method of pushing gas in through the vent line; it fell only to about 92%.
sources: Lovell, 'Houston, We've Had a Problem', Apollo Expeditions to the Moon, NASA SP-350 (1975), ch.13.1, https://apolloexplorer.co.uk/books/sp-350/ch-13-1.html

timeline.event: Special detanking. The tank heaters were switched on from the 65 V dc ground supply, with the fans added after about 1.5 h, followed by pressure/vent cycling. The heaters ran for about 8 hours in total. As the thermostatic switches tried to open at their 80 F limit, the 65 V arc welded them shut. The heater tube reached an estimated ~1,000 F (~538 C) in spots, which badly damaged the Teflon insulation on the fan-motor wires. From then on, in the Board's words, the tank was 'in a hazardous condition when filled with oxygen and electrically powered.'
sources: Review Board report pp.4-21 to 4-23 and finding l

timeline.event: Fill test. Both tanks were filled to about 20%. Emptying tank no. 2 again needed pressure cycling with the heaters on. Managers were focused on the loose fill tube rather than the long heater runs, and decided to fly the tank as it was. Replacing the shelf would have taken at least 45 hours.

Backup crewman Charlie Duke exposed the crews to rubella, and prime CMP Ken Mattingly turned out to have no immunity. Backup CMP Jack Swigert replaced him. The Mission Report says the final decision came 'on the day prior to launch'; its summary says 'two days before launch'. Mattingly never developed rubella.
sources: Apollo 13 Mission Report MSC-02680, sec. 1.0 and 9.3, https://apollojournals.org/afj/ap13fj/pdf/a13-mission-report-197007.pdf

timeline.event: Launch from LC-39A. Range zero was 19:13:00 GMT and lift-off 19:13:00.65 GMT. The S-II center engine shut down about 132 s early because of pogo oscillation; the other engines burned about 34 s longer to compensate.
sources: Apollo 13 Postlaunch Mission Operations Report M-932-70-13, https://apollojournals.org/afj/ap13fj/pdf/a13-postlaunch-mission-ops-report-19700428.pdf

timeline.event: Translunar injection burn of the S-IVB.

The first midcourse correction (MCC-2, an SPS burn) moved Apollo 13 off a free-return trajectory onto a 'hybrid' trajectory for Fra Mauro. From this point the spacecraft would NOT have come home on its own.

Lovell closed the TV broadcast: '...this is the crew of Apollo 13 wishing everybody there a nice evening, and we're just about ready to close out our inspection of Aquarius and get back for a pleasant evening in Odyssey. Good night.' None of the major US networks carried the broadcast live.
sources: Apollo 13 Flight Journal, Day 3 'Before the storm', https://apollojournals.org/afj/ap13fj/07day3-before-the-storm.html

timeline.event: The ground asked for a cryo stir, and the crew acknowledged at 55:53:06. Swigert switched on the tank 1 fans at 55:53:18 and the tank 2 fans at 55:53:20. Tank 2 pressure then rose abnormally, peaking at 1,008.3 psia at 55:54:45.

Oxygen tank no. 2 failed. Sudden accelerometer activity began at 55:54:53.182, followed by 1.8 s of telemetry loss and a Main Bus B undervolt master alarm. The bay 4 outer panel blew off, the high-gain antenna was damaged, and tank no. 1's high-pressure system started leaking. Fuel cells 1 and 3 lost their oxygen flow by 55:55:01. The Mission Report and Board list the official 'cryogenic oxygen tank incident' time as 55:54:53.
sources: Review Board report Table 4-II and finding n

timeline.event: The 'problem' calls. Per the corrected transcript, which used voice identification, Swigert said 'Okay, Houston...', Lovell overlapped with 'Houston...', and Swigert finished '...we've had a problem here.' CAPCOM Jack Lousma (55:55:28): 'This is Houston. Say again, please.' Lovell (55:55:35): 'Houston, we've had a problem. We've had a Main B Bus Undervolt.' The 1970 NASA technical transcript instead gives 'LMP: Okay, Houston --' and 'CDR: I believe we've had a problem here.' The 55:55:35 Lovell line is the same in both.
sources: Apollo 13 Technical Air-to-Ground Voice Transcription (1970), tape 36/14 p.161, https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/as13-tec.pdf
Lovell, NASA SP-350 ch.13.1 (credits Swigert with the first call)

timeline.event: Haise: 'Okay. Right now, Houston, the voltage is - is looking good. And we had a pretty large bang associated with the Caution and Warning there.'

Lovell: '...it looks to me, looking out the hatch, that we are venting something. We are - We are venting something out into the - into space.' Then: 'It's a gas of some sort.' Flight Director Kranz on the flight loop: 'Crew thinks they are venting something!'
Lousma (with Glynn Lunney's team now on console): 'It's slowly going to zero, and we're starting to think about the LM lifeboat.' Swigert: 'Yes. That's what we're thinking about, too.'
sources: Apollo 13 Flight Journal, Day 3 part 3 'Aquarius becomes a lifeboat', https://apollojournals.org/afj/ap13fj/09day3-lifeboat.html

timeline.event: Lifeboat power-up. At 57:36:12 Lousma said there was about 15 minutes of power left in the CM; this meant the last fuel cell's oxygen, not the entry batteries. At 57:41:38 Swigert reported 'Fred and Jim are in the LM', and at 57:41:47 Haise said 'I got LM power on.' At about 58:00:39 Haise added 'Didn't think I'd be back (in) this soon.' Around 58:09 Lovell read out the CM and LM gimbal angles for the hand-computed platform transfer, and from about 58:15 Swigert powered the CM down. The Mission Report says LM activation finished just as fuel cell 2's reactant flow went to zero.

Descent-engine burn on the docked stack: 34.2 s, 37.8 ft/s. It put Apollo 13 back on a free return, which on its own would have brought a landing in the Indian Ocean at about 152 h GET. Lovell later wrote 'ground-computed 35-second burn... 5 hours after the explosion'.

Far-side pass with about 25 minutes of loss of signal. LOS came about 77:08-77:09 and Lovell said 'Good morning, Houston' at AOS at 77:33:50. Closest approach was roughly 136-137 nmi (~254 km) above the far side. Apollo 13's crew became the farthest humans from Earth: 400,171 km per Guinness, about 400,04x km in other reconstructions. Artemis II broke the record on 6 Apr 2026. The exact pericynthion GET (~77:2x) was not re-verified from the primary table, whose OCR is garbled.
sources: NASA SVS 'Simulating the Artemis II Lunar Flyby on April 6, 2026', https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/5633

timeline.event: The S-IVB stage hit the Moon 74 nmi from the Apollo 12 seismometer. At 78:02:44 Lovell said: 'Well, at least something worked on this flight.'

PC+2 transearth injection on the descent engine: 263.8 s (Mission Report; the Mission Operations Report says 263.4 s), 860.5 ft/s. It moved the landing from the Indian Ocean (~152 h) to the mid-Pacific (predicted 142:53). The Mission Report says this cut the transearth time by 'about 9 hours'; the AFJ says ~10 h and Wikipedia says 12 h. Before the burn the crew had checked the LM platform at about 73:46-74 h by sighting the Sun, because debris made star sightings impractical.
sources: Mission Report sec. 4 and Table 4-III, sec. 8.7.5

timeline.event: CAPCOM Vance Brand (80:22:13) said the planned CO2 fix 'will look like a mailbox, when you get it all put together.' Haise (80:37:33) asked what material 'to build this mailbox out of'. At 80:30:53 the LM CO2 caution light came on at the nominal 7.6 mmHg limit.

With the medical limit raised to 15 mmHg, the LM's CO2 partial pressure was allowed to climb: 10.7 at 82:25; 11.3 on the ground gauge and ~12.5 onboard at 82:53; 'just below 13' at 83:28; and 14.9 indicated before the switch to the LM secondary cartridge at about 85:26 (~02:39 CST 15 Apr). After the switch it fell to 4.6.

CAPCOM Joe Kerwin read up the canister-adapter procedure step by step and Swigert built it, helped by Lovell and Haise. At 91:10:26 Swigert said: 'Okay. Our do-it-yourself lithium hydroxide canister change is complete.' At 91:12:30 Kerwin said the ground was reading 4.7 mmHg and asked them to build a second unit on the commander's hose.
sources: Apollo 13 Flight Journal, Day 4 part 4 'Building the CO2 adapter', https://apollojournals.org/afj/ap13fj/15day4-mailbox.html

timeline.event: After a look into the powered-down CM, Swigert said: 'I'll tell you, Deke, it's cold up in there. I don't know whether we'll be able to sleep up there tonight; it must be about 35 or 40 degrees.' (Fahrenheit, about 2-4 C.)
sources: Apollo 13 Flight Journal, Day 5 part 2 'Feeling the cold', https://apollojournals.org/afj/ap13fj/18day5-feelingthecold.html

timeline.event: Manual midcourse correction MCC-5 on the descent engine at 10% throttle: 14 s (Mission Report; the Mission Operations Report says 15 s), about 7.8 ft/s, to steepen the entry angle. With the LM guidance platform powered down, the crew aligned the stack by putting the cusps of Earth's terminator on the alignment-sight reticle and holding the Sun in the telescope. Haise flew pitch, Lovell flew roll, the abort guidance system held yaw, and Swigert called the start and stop times. The engine was cut 1 s early to avoid an overburn.
A second CM canister was added in series to each adapter, which Kerwin called 'your friendly do-it-yourself kit'. PPCO2 fell from 1.8 to 0.8 mmHg and afterwards stayed around 0.1-0.3 mmHg.

Ken Mattingly, now CAPCOM, read up the CM reactivation/power-up procedures. EECOM John Aaron was part of the team that wrote them. Lovell later wrote that Mission Control produced them in three days 'instead of the usual three months'.
Final midcourse correction MCC-7 on the LM RCS thrusters: 21.5 s (Mission Report; the Mission Operations Report says 22.4 s), 3.0 ft/s. Attitude was again set by hand using Earth as the reference.

Service module jettison, about 4 h 39 min before entry; Lovell's voice call 'SM Sep' is logged at 138:02:06. At 138:04:46 Lovell said: 'And there's one whole side of that spacecraft missing.' At 138:04:57: 'Right by the - Look out there, will you? Right by the high gain antenna, the whole panel is blown out, almost from the base to the engine.' Haise (138:05:31): 'It's really a mess.' Haise (138:09:09): 'Man, that's unbelievable!'
The command module Odyssey was powered up again. Its entry batteries had been recharged from LM power: battery A took 15 h and B about 3 h.

Lunar module undocking/jettison, about 1 h 11 min before entry. Tunnel pressure pushed the LM away. Swigert counted down '10 seconds', Lovell called 'Five. LM jettison.', and CAPCOM Joe Kerwin said at 141:30:05: 'Okay, copy that. Farewell, Aquarius, and we thank you.'
Swigert: 'I know all of us here want to thank all you guys down there for the very fine job you did.' Lovell: 'That's affirm, Joe.'

Kerwin: 'Okay LOS is about a minute or a minute and a half; in entry attitude, we'd like Omni Charlie, and welcome home. Over.' Swigert: 'Thank you.' These were the last crew words before loss of signal and blackout.

Entry interface at 400,000 ft (Mission Report; the Mission Operations Report says 142:40:47). The final entry PAD gave 36,211 ft/s (~11.0 km/s) at a flight-path angle of 6.20 deg, with blackout predicted to start at EI+0:19 (~142:41:05) and end at EI+3:38 (~142:44:24). Predicted peak load was 5.2 g.
sources: Apollo 13 Flight Journal, Day 6 part 8 (entry PAD and PAO commentary)

timeline.event: Signal came back later than predicted. The PAO reported that the ARIA 4 aircraft had acquisition of signal; Kerwin called at 142:46:03 'Odyssey, Houston standing by. Over.' and Swigert answered at 142:46:08 'Okay, Joe.' That first voice came about 1 min 44 s after the predicted end of blackout, about 5 min after the predicted start, and about 7 min 23 s after the last pre-blackout words. The cause of the delay is DISPUTED; see key facts.
Swigert: 'We got two good drogues.' Kerwin (142:50:06): 'Odyssey, Houston. We show you on the mains, it really looks great.' Kerwin (142:50:15): 'Got you on television, babe.'

Splashdown in the South Pacific southeast of American Samoa at 21deg38'24"S, 165deg21'42"W per the Mission Report (the Mission Operations Report gives ~21deg40'S, 165deg22'W). The CM landed upright (stable 1), about 1 nmi from the target and about 3.5 nmi (6.5 km) from the recovery ship USS Iwo Jima, within sight of it. Total flight time was 142:54:41.
sources: Apollo 13 Flight Journal, Day 6 part 8 (recovery loop: '3 1/2 miles Iwo Jima')

timeline.event: A helicopter delivered the crew aboard USS Iwo Jima within 45 minutes of landing, the fastest recovery of any crewed Apollo flight.
Aquarius re-entered and came down in the open sea between Samoa and New Zealand at about 25.5 S, 176 W, carrying the SNAP-27 radioisotope fuel capsule for the lunar experiment package.

President Nixon presented the Presidential Medal of Freedom to the Mission Operations Team in Houston (accepted by Sigurd Sjoberg, with flight directors Kranz, Lunney, Griffin and Windler on stage), then flew to Honolulu and presented it to the three astronauts.
NASA appointed the Apollo 13 Review Board, chaired by Edgar M. Cortright with Neil Armstrong as a member, on 17 Apr 1970. Its report, dated 15 June 1970, judged the accident 'nearly catastrophic'.
sources: Review Board report (memoranda of 17 and 21 Apr 1970; ch.5)

timeline.event: Apollo 14 launched to Fra Mauro with a redesigned oxygen system: a third O2 tank in bay 1, no fans in the tanks, stainless-steel-sheathed wiring, and a ~400 Ah emergency battery in the SM.

key_facts.fact: Names: crew Commander James A. Lovell Jr. (42), Command Module Pilot John L. 'Jack' Swigert Jr. (38) and Lunar Module Pilot Fred W. Haise Jr. (36). The command module was 'Odyssey' and the lunar module 'Aquarius'. CAPCOMs heard in key moments: Jack Lousma (explosion), Vance Brand ('mailbox' remark), Joe Kerwin (adapter read-up, LM farewell, entry), Deke Slayton (102 h cold remark) and Ken Mattingly (CM reactivation read-up).
sources: Apollo 13 Flight Journal pages cited in timeline

key_facts.fact: Time convention: GET (ground elapsed time) runs from range zero at 19:13:00 GMT on 11 Apr 1970. Houston was on CST (UTC-6) in April 1970 because daylight time started 26 Apr. Explosion: 55:54:53 GET = 21:07:53 CST on 13 Apr = 03:07:53 UTC on 14 Apr = 12:07 KST on 14 Apr. Launch at 13:13 CST and the 13 April explosion date are true only in Houston time; in Korea the explosion fell on 14 April. The 1970 technical transcript writes times as DD HH MM SS, so '02 07 55 35' means 55:55:35 GET.
sources: Lovell, NASA SP-350 ch.13.1 ('1313 Houston time'; 'The time was 2108 hours on April 13')

key_facts.fact: Distance from Earth at the explosion: PAO readouts gave 177,861 nmi (329,399 km) at 55:47 GET and 178,643 nmi (330,847 km) at 56:12 GET, so about 178,000 nmi, roughly 330,000 km or 205,000 statute miles. Lovell's SP-350 account and NASA pages round this to 'about 200,000 miles'. The figure of 320,000 km that sometimes appears is only a conversion of that rounded 200,000 miles. Best wording for Korean narration: '지구에서 약 33만 km'. Minor caveat: PAO figures are display 'altitude' values and may be measured from Earth's center, which would differ by about 2%; this does not change the rounding.
sources: Apollo 13 Flight Journal, Day 3 parts 1-2 (PAO commentary), https://apollojournals.org/afj/ap13fj/08day3-problem.html

key_facts.fact: Cause, from the Review Board. Thermostatic switches rated for 28 V dc failed under 65 V dc ground power during an improvised 8-hour detanking at KSC on 27 Mar 1970: they welded shut, the heater tube reached about 1,000 F (~538 C), and the Teflon insulation on the fan wires was damaged. That detanking was needed because a probably loose fill tube, possibly jarred in the 21 Oct 1968 shelf drop of about 2 inches (5 cm), stopped the tank emptying normally. In flight, the fan wiring, possibly moved by the stir, short-circuited and ignited its insulation. The fire in high-pressure oxygen overheated the conduit and failed the tank, blowing off the bay 4 panel and damaging tank 1's plumbing. The Board's summary: 'not the result of a chance malfunction... but rather resulted from an unusual combination of mistakes, coupled with a somewhat deficient and unforgiving design.'
sources: Review Board report ch.4 pp.4-20 to 4-23, ch.5 findings a-n

key_facts.fact: There were about 93 s between Swigert switching on the tank 2 fans (55:53:20) and the tank failure (55:54:53). Telemetry dropped out for 1.8 s. Tank 1 leaked down over roughly 2-3 h, and the Mission Report says it held enough pressure to keep fuel cell 2 running about 2 more hours. NSSDCA: 'All oxygen stores were lost within about 3 hours.'

Where the crew were at the bang, from the 1970 technical debrief quoted in the AFJ: Swigert in the left-hand couch, Lovell in the lower equipment bay, Haise coming up from the LM. Lovell: 'There was a dull but definite bang - not much of a vibration'. Haise: 'I felt just a slight shudder.'
sources: Apollo 13 Flight Journal, Day 3 part 2 (quoting 1970 Technical Crew Debriefing)

key_facts.fact: Exact wording of the famous line. Lovell at 55:55:35: 'Houston, we've had a problem. We've had a Main B Bus Undervolt.' This is agreed in both the 1970 NASA technical transcript and the corrected Flight Journal. The first call at 55:55:19-20 is DISPUTED as to speaker and wording. The AFJ, using voice identification, gives Swigert: 'Okay, Houston... we've had a problem here' (with Lovell overlapping 'Houston'). The 1970 transcript gives 'Okay, Houston --' (labelled LMP) and 'I believe we've had a problem here' (labelled CDR). Lovell himself credits Swigert. For subtitles, the safest clip is Lovell's 55:55:35 line.

LM design limits versus what was actually needed. Lovell: 'the LM was built for only a 45-hour lifetime, and we had to stretch that to 90' and 'The LM was designed to support two men for two days. Now it was being asked to care for three men nearly four days.' In practice Aquarius supported three men from power-up (~57:42 GET) to undocking (141:30), about 84 h. The Mission Report gives an '82-hour period' for LM oxygen use.

How the LM consumables were stretched: (1) Power was cut to about 350-400 W (about 12 A) and the LM guidance computer and platform were switched off for most of the coast; Lovell says energy use fell to 'a fifth of normal' and about 20% of the 2,181 Ah of LM battery capacity was left at jettison. (2) A slow 'passive thermal control' roll was set up by hand. (3) Water was rationed. (4) The CM entry batteries were recharged from LM power. (5) Overboard dumps were banned after one urine dump, so urine was stowed in bags. (6) CM lithium hydroxide canisters were adapted for the LM. Oxygen was never the limiting consumable.

Oxygen: the LM used 20.3 lb of O2 over about 82 h (0.25 lb/h), with 33.5 lb left at undocking (Mission Report). Lovell's account says 28.5 lb, 'more than half of what we started with'. The small difference is between sources; either way, oxygen was never close to running out.

Water and rationing. The CM potable tank held about 38 lb at the incident, and the crew drew about 14 lb into juice bags. LM water was 338 lb loaded, mostly for sublimator cooling, with about 290 lb used. Remaining at undocking: the Mission Report says about 50 lb indicated, Lovell says 28.2 lb (about 9%); this is DISPUTED between sources. Haise calculated they might run out of cooling water about 5 h before entry. Rationing: Mission Report, 'Not more than 24 ounces of water were consumed by each crewman after the incident'; Lovell, 'six ounces each per day, a fifth of normal intake' (about 180 mL/day). The two figures agree. They drank juice to keep electrolytes up and ate only foods that needed no water. The CM potable tank seemed empty about 24 h before entry, but postflight 24.3 lb was drained from it; the lines had most likely frozen.

Haise's illness: the Mission Report says Haise had a urinary tract infection at recovery and dizzy spells postflight, linked to fatigue, weightlessness and the infection. The AFJ says it was bacterial, treated with antibiotics, and that he was feverish on the final day. SP-350 says he was 'invalided three weeks by infection'. Later popular accounts call it a 'kidney infection' with a high fever, which is NOT in the 1970 Mission Report. Weight losses: Lovell 14 lb, Swigert 11 lb, Haise 6.5 lb, 31.5 lb in total, an Apollo record per Lovell.

Cabin temperatures, which vary by source and by module. Command module: 'slowly decreased to approximately 43 F' (6 C) per the Mission Report; Swigert estimated '35 or 40 degrees' F (2-4 C) at 102:10; the AFJ commentary near 123 h gives 7.2-7.8 C; Lovell's later account says 'the temperature dropped to 38 F' (3 C). Lunar module: 'typically between 54 and 60 F' (12-16 C) per the Mission Report; PAO read 51-52 F (~11 C) at 120-124 h. The CM became too cold to sleep in, and per the Mission Report the LM 'cooled down to an extent where sleep was not possible for approximately the last 16 hours.' The cabins were cold, but there is no primary source for below-freezing cabin air.
sources: Apollo 13 Flight Journal, Day 5 part 2 and Day 6 part 1 (PAO)

key_facts.fact: Condensation: the CM windows were 'nearly opaque with water droplets' by about 73 h, and by about 110 h a thin film of water covered the CM interior structure and the LM windows. Lovell: the CM walls, panels and wire harnesses were covered in droplets at power-up, and during deceleration 'it rained inside the CM.' Thanks to post-Apollo 1 wiring safeguards, there was no arcing.

Sleep: no crewman slept from the incident until about 80 h GET. Estimated total sleep from the incident to splashdown was about 11 h for Lovell, 12 h for Swigert and 19 h for Haise. The Mission Report's OCR is slightly garbled for Lovell's figure.

CO2 levels: the normal CO2 caution limit was 7.6 mmHg and was raised by medical decision to 15 mmHg. The LM primary LiOH cartridge, rated for 41 man-hours, was used for about 27 h (82 man-hours). The indicated peak was 14.9 mmHg just before the switch to the secondary cartridge at about 85.5 h. CO2 was above 7.6 mmHg for only about 4 h (Mission Report; transcript readings suggest roughly 80.5 to 85.5 h). Mission Report: 'no adverse physiological effects or degradation in crew performance resulted.' With the CM canisters in the adapter, PPCO2 stayed between 0.1 and 1.8 mmHg for the rest of the flight. A PAO remark noted that MSC test subjects had tolerated up to 22 mmHg.
sources: Apollo 13 Flight Journal, Day 4 parts 2-4 and Day 5

key_facts.fact: The 'mailbox' adapter. The problem was that the CM's square LiOH canisters did not fit the LM's round cartridge sockets. The procedure, read up by Kerwin from 90:22:50 and first unit complete at 91:10:26, used: two CM LiOH canisters; strips of gray duct tape wrapped sticky side out as belts; the plastic bags that the liquid-cooling garments came packed in; a cardboard LM EVA cue card bent into an arch so the bag would not be sucked onto the screen; a red suit O2 hose pushed into a hole cut in the bag; and a towel, wet wipe, sock piece or crumpled tape to plug the canister's bypass hole. The suit fans drew cabin air through it. Later a second canister was taped in series on each unit. It was designed by MSC Crew Systems Division (Ed Smylie, Jim Correale, with procedures by Tony England), and per the Mission Report it was 'assembled and tested on the ground during the flight prior to its actual use in the spacecraft.' Vance Brand first called it a 'mailbox' on air at 80:22:13.
sources: Apollo 13 Flight Journal, Day 4 part 2 and part 4, https://apollojournals.org/afj/ap13fj/15day4-mailbox.html

key_facts.fact: Trajectory facts. Apollo 13 had been off free-return since 30:40:50. The 61:29:43 descent-engine burn (34.2 s) restored a free return, but that path led to an Indian Ocean landing at about 152 h. The PC+2 burn at 79:27:39 (263.8 s, 860.5 ft/s) shortened the trip and moved the landing to the Pacific. Further corrections followed: MCC-5 at 105:18:28 (manual, using the Earth's terminator, about 14 s at 10% throttle) and MCC-7 at 137:39:52 (LM RCS, 21.5 s). Popular summaries often merge the two manual burns into one.

Why the service module stayed attached until 138 h: Mission Control kept it as long as possible to shield the CM heat shield from the cold of space. Lovell wrote that 'everyone feared what the cold of space might do to the unsheltered CM heat shield.' On separation the crew first saw that the bay 4 panel was missing, with debris hanging out and possible staining on the SPS engine bell.

Re-entry blackout, DISPUTED. The final entry PAD predicted blackout from EI+0:19 to EI+3:38, about 3 min 19 s. In practice the first crew voice ('Okay, Joe', 142:46:08) came about 1 min 44 s after the predicted end. Measured from the last pre-entry words (142:38:45) the silence was about 7 min 23 s, because the ground station also lost line of sight before entry. Popular claims such as 'normally 4 minutes, this time 6' or '87 seconds longer' cannot be checked against a primary figure. The usual explanation, a shallow entry angle (~-6.2 deg), is described by the Flight Journal editors as 'a favorite topic of speculation', which 'the original reports do not pay any heed to'. Reacquisition also depended on ARIA relay aircraft. Recommended wording: 'radio contact came back later than predicted, about one and a half minutes'.

Splashdown and recovery: 142:54:41 GET (13:07:41 EST, 17 Apr 1970) at 21deg38'24"S, 165deg21'42"W, about 1 nmi from target and about 3.5 nmi from USS Iwo Jima. Weather was broken stratus at 2,000 ft with 1-2 ft waves. The crew were aboard the ship at 13:53 EST, under 45 minutes after landing, the fastest crewed Apollo recovery. From explosion to splashdown was 86 h 59 min 48 s, about 87 hours.

Crew words that are reliably attributed and usable as short clips, each confirmed in both the AFJ and the 1970 technical transcript:
- 55:55:35 Lovell: 'Houston, we've had a problem. We've had a Main B Bus Undervolt.'
- 55:56:10 Haise: 'we had a pretty large bang'
- 56:09:07 Lovell: 'we are venting something out into the - into space'
- 56:09:29 Lovell: 'It's a gas of some sort.'
- 57:24:20 Swigert: 'That's what we're thinking about, too'
- 91:10:26 Swigert: 'Our do-it-yourself lithium hydroxide canister change is complete.'
- 102:10:42 Swigert: 'it's cold up in there'
- 138:04:46 Lovell: 'And there's one whole side of that spacecraft missing.'
- 138:09:09 Haise: 'Man, that's unbelievable!'
- 141:30:05 Kerwin (CAPCOM, not crew): 'Farewell, Aquarius, and we thank you.'
- 142:46:08 Swigert: 'Okay, Joe.'
- 142:49:17 Swigert: 'We got two good drogues.'

Audio availability. The Apollo Flight Journal, now hosted at apollojournals.org because the old history.nasa.gov/afj links redirect to a NASA landing page, serves directly downloadable MP3 clips named by start GET. For example, https://apollojournals.org/afj/ap13fj/audio/a13_0555519.mp3 (starts at 055:55:19) returned HTTP 200, 128 kbps stereo, 6 min 19 s. There are about 549 audio links across the AFJ pages, some marked -pao (Public Affairs commentary) or -ag (air-to-ground). key_facts.fact: The 80 F gauge detail is a minor dispute. NSSDCA says the in-tank temperature gauges 'were designed to measure only to 80 F, so the extreme heating was not noticed.' Wikipedia (citing Chaikin) says 85 F. The Review Board itself says only that the switches were set to open at 80 F and that the temperature indication 'rose past 80 F'. Recommendation: leave the gauge limit out of the reel.

facts.aftermath:
The crew stayed overnight on USS Iwo Jima, flew to Pago Pago and then Honolulu. On 18 Apr 1970 President Nixon gave the Presidential Medal of Freedom to the Mission Operations Team in Houston (accepted by Sigurd Sjoberg) and to the three astronauts in Honolulu. Odyssey was offloaded in Hawaii on 24 Apr and returned to North American Rockwell in Downey on 27 Apr. Aquarius burned up and fell into the sea between Samoa and New Zealand (~25.5 S, 176 W), carrying its SNAP-27 plutonium fuel capsule.

Investigation: NASA formed the Apollo 13 Review Board, chaired by Edgar M. Cortright with Neil Armstrong as a member, on 17 Apr 1970. Its report, dated 15 Jun 1970, traced the failure to the 28 V/65 V thermostatic-switch mismatch, the improvised 8-hour heater detanking on 27 Mar 1970, and damaged Teflon wire insulation. The board called the accident 'nearly catastrophic', saved only by 'outstanding performance on the part of the crew, Mission Control, and other members of the team.'

Changes for Apollo 14 onward:
- No fans in the oxygen tanks, and Teflon replaced with non-flammable materials.
- Wiring sheathed in stainless steel and a redesigned heater.
- A third cryogenic oxygen tank in SM bay 1, away from bay 4.
- A ~400 Ah emergency battery in the SM, plus fuel-cell valve changes.

Apollo 14 launched on 31 Jan 1971, about 9 months later, and landed at Fra Mauro, Apollo 13's original target.

The crew afterwards:
- Lovell never flew again. He co-wrote 'Lost Moon' (1994), the basis for Ron Howard's 1995 film, and died on 7 Aug 2025 in Lake Forest, Illinois, aged 97.
- Swigert left NASA, was elected to the US House from Colorado in 1982, and died of cancer before taking office, aged 51.
- Haise flew the Space Shuttle Enterprise approach-and-landing tests in 1977 and published the memoir 'Never Panic Early'. As of 2025-2026 reporting he is the last surviving Apollo 13 crew member, still giving talks in April 2026.

Apollo 13 kept the record for the farthest humans from Earth (~400,171 km per Guinness) until Artemis II passed it on 6 Apr 2026.

A light anecdote from Lovell's SP-350 caption: Grumman jokingly sent North American Rockwell a 'towing' bill of more than $400,000.
myths: MYTH: 'Houston, we have a problem.' FACT: Lovell said 'Houston, we've had a problem. We've had a Main B Bus Undervolt' at 55:55:35. Just before that, Swigert said 'Okay, Houston... we've had a problem here', or 'I believe we've had a problem here' in the 1970 transcript. The present tense comes from the 1995 film. Keep 'we've had' in English subtitles.

MYTH: Gene Kranz said 'Failure is not an option' during the mission. FACT: no transcript or loop recording has it. The line came from FIDO Jerry Bostick telling the screenwriters (Al Reinert, Bill Broyles) that 'failure was not one of' the options. It became the film's tagline, spoken by Ed Harris, and later the title of Kranz's 2000 memoir.
MYTH: Lovell (or the crew) said 'Farewell, Aquarius, and we thank you.' FACT: CAPCOM Joe Kerwin said it from Houston at 141:30:05, right after Lovell called 'LM jettison'.

MYTH: they were about to run out of oxygen. FACT: oxygen was never the limiting consumable; 33.5 lb of LM O2 was left at undocking (Mission Report). The real limits were CO2 removal, electrical power and cooling water.

MYTH: CO2 poisoning nearly killed the crew, and the 'mailbox' was built at the last second. FACT: the CO2 limit was medically raised to 15 mmHg and the indicated peak was 14.9 mmHg (about 85 h) before they switched to the LM's secondary cartridge. The adapter was built at 90:22-91:10 GET while the reading was about 4.7 mmHg, because the LM's own cartridges would not last the trip. The Mission Report says there were no adverse physiological effects.

MYTH: the astronauts invented the adapter themselves from whatever was lying around. FACT: MSC Crew Systems Division engineers designed it, built it and tested it on the ground. CAPCOM Kerwin then read it up step by step (about 48 minutes for the first unit), and Swigert built it with Lovell and Haise.

MYTH: the free-return trajectory would carry them home automatically. FACT: Apollo 13 had left free return at 30:40:50. It took a 34-second LM descent-engine burn at 61:29:43 to get back on one, which still pointed to the Indian Ocean at about 152 h. The PC+2 burn then moved the landing to the Pacific.

MYTH: the spacecraft cabin was below freezing. FACT: the CM fell to about 43 F / 6 C (Mission Report); crew estimates were 35-40 F (2-4 C) and Lovell later wrote 38 F (3 C). The LM, where they lived, was about 51-60 F (11-16 C). It was miserably cold and wet, but not below freezing.

MYTH: the explosion happened at 200,000 miles / 320,000 km. FACT: 200,000 miles is a round figure. NASA PAO readouts put the spacecraft at about 178,000 nautical miles, roughly 330,000 km or 205,000 statute miles.

MYTH: dropping the tank in 1968 caused the explosion. FACT: the Review Board treated the 2-inch shelf drop only as the PROBABLE cause of a loose fill tube. That led to the improvised 65 V heater detanking, which welded the 28 V-rated thermostatic switches shut and cooked the Teflon insulation. That overheating was the decisive damage.
MYTH: a meteoroid hit Apollo 13. FACT: this was the crew's first guess in the minutes after the bang. The investigation found a fire inside oxygen tank no. 2.

MYTH: the blackout 'normally 4 minutes' lasted 6 'because of the shallow entry'. FACT: the predicted blackout was about 3 min 19 s, and the first crew voice came about 1 min 44 s after its predicted end. The official reports give no cause; the shallow-angle explanation is speculation.
MYTH: Apollo 13 still holds the record for the farthest humans from Earth. FACT: it held the record from 1970 until Artemis II passed it on 6 April 2026.

MYTH: one manual 'terminator' burn saved them. FACT: there were two hand-flown corrections. MCC-5 at 105:18:28 used the descent engine for 14 s, aligned on Earth's terminator. MCC-7 at 137:39:52 used the RCS thrusters for 21.5 s.

MYTH: Ken Mattingly alone worked out the CM power-up in the simulator. FACT: a ground team including EECOM John Aaron wrote the reactivation procedures. Mattingly helped and read them up as CAPCOM at about 126 h GET. He never caught rubella and later flew Apollo 16.

MYTH: Gene Kranz single-handedly ran the rescue. FACT: four flight control teams, led by Kranz, Lunney, Griffin and Windler, worked in rotation. Lunney's team was on console when the lifeboat decision went up at 57:24. The Medal of Freedom went to the whole Mission Operations Team.

MYTH: Haise had a severe kidney infection. FACT: the 1970 Mission Report records a urinary tract infection, and the AFJ adds that he was feverish on the last day. 'Kidney infection' and specific fever numbers come from later accounts, so treat them as unverified.

MYTH: the service module was cast off right after the explosion. FACT: it stayed attached until 138:01:48, about 4.5 h before entry, to protect the CM heat shield from the cold of space. Only then did the crew see the missing panel.
facts.sensitivities:
Real people and deaths:
- Lovell died 7 Aug 2025 (aged 97) and Swigert in 1982 (aged 51).
- Haise is alive (born 14 Nov 1933) and, per 2025-2026 reporting, is the last surviving crew member.
- Do not imply that all three are gone, or that Haise is.

Speech, thoughts and translation:
- Never invent inner thoughts, fear or dialogue. Use only transcript words, each tagged with its GET, in English with a Korean subtitle.
- Mark the CAPCOM as speaking from Houston: 'Farewell, Aquarius' is Kerwin's line.
- In Korean, the misquote and the real line look almost the same ('휴스턴, 문제가 생겼다'). Show the English 'we've had a problem' on screen with a brief note that the film's 'we have' is a misquote.
- Do not present 'Failure is not an option' as something said in 1970.

Audio:
- Use only NASA mission audio (air-to-ground, PAO, or the Flight Director loop clearly labelled). No 1995 film or documentary audio or music, and do not copy the film's staging or iconic shots.

NASA material and branding:
- NASA audio, transcripts and most imagery are not copyrighted. NASA media guidelines still forbid using the NASA insignia or 'meatball' logo or implying NASA endorsement, and they restrict commercial use of astronauts' likenesses. Code-drawn, faceless illustrations fit this.
- Leave out the NASA logo and the Apollo 13 mission patch, and credit 'Audio: NASA (public domain)'.

Numbers:
- Use the primary-source figures and say 'about': ~330,000 km, ~87 hours from explosion to splashdown, CM about 3-6 C, CO2 limit raised to 15 mmHg.
- Avoid 'near-lethal CO2', 'below freezing' and 'six-minute blackout caused by shallow entry' as hard claims.

Time zones:
- The famous 13:13 launch and 13 April explosion are Houston (CST) times. In Korea the explosion fell at about 12:07 on 14 April.

Medical:
- Haise's urinary tract infection and the stowed urine bags are fine to mention briefly, without graphic detail.
- Avoid saying the crew 'nearly died of CO2'; the Mission Report records no adverse effects.

Apollo 1:
- A brief nod to post-1967 wiring safeguards is fine, but don't sensationalize those deaths.

The word 'explosion':
- NASA and Lovell use it, but technically it was an internal fire that ruptured the tank. 'Exploded' is acceptable in narration.

quotes.speaker: Fred Haise (LMP)
quotes.words_en: There she goes, gang. The Moon.
quotes.context: GET 080:36:25 (AFJ). Preceded by 'No. He didn't want it.' The receding Moon (the lost landing). Onboard/VOX remark captured on the loop.
quotes.korean: 저기 간다, 다들. 달이.

quotes.speaker: Fred Haise (LMP)
quotes.words_en: Okay, Houston. We just got a Master Alarm and an ECS light. I take it the partial pressure CO2 is - yeah - that's what tripped it.
quotes.context: GET 080:30:53. First CO2 warning in the LM. AFJ: the CO2 component light is set to trip at 7.6 mmHg. Lovell 080:31:20: 'Oh what was that? CO2? All right. CO2 value is getting high.'
quotes.korean: 휴스턴, 방금 마스터 알람과 ECS 경고등이 켜졌습니다. 이산화탄소 분압 때문인 것 같네요. 네, 그게 원인입니다.

quotes.speaker: Vance Brand (CAPCOM)
quotes.words_en: Yes. We wish we could send you a kit and it would be kind of like putting a model airplane together or something. As it turns out, this contraption will look like a mailbox, when you get it all put together.
quotes.context: GET 080:22:13. Origin of the 'mailbox' name for the square-to-round LiOH canister adapter. Haise replies 'What do we make it out of, Vance?' and Brand answers '...with a plastic roof.'
quotes.korean: 키트로 보내 드릴 수 있으면 좋겠네요. 모형 비행기 조립하는 거랑 비슷할 겁니다. 다 조립하고 나면 이 장치는 우편함처럼 생기게 될 겁니다.

quotes.speaker: Fred Haise (LMP)
quotes.words_en: Okay. You guys just tell me what sort of material you had in mind to build this mailbox out of, and Jack and I will go to work on trying to construct that thing. Assume we'll use the space-age baling wire or the gray tape?
quotes.context: GET 080:37:33. The crew's first use of 'mailbox'. 'Gray tape' = duct tape.
quotes.korean: 이 우편함을 뭘로 만들 생각인지만 알려 주세요. 잭이랑 제가 만들어 보겠습니다. 우주 시대 철사 끈이나 회색 테이프를 쓰는 거겠죠?

quotes.speaker: Vance Brand (CAPCOM)
quotes.words_en: ...in short, you use plastic as a covering for the whole thing. You put some kind of a stiffener at the top so the plastic doesn't suck against the ... LiOH ... entrance side. You need gray tape to stick the whole thing together, and you need something like a sock to put in the - the bottom so that the outlet side is plugged up.
quotes.context: GET 080:37:51. Outline of the adapter (abridged; the original has a self-correction 'LOI - LiOH enter - entrance side').
quotes.korean: 요약하면, 전체를 비닐로 씌웁니다. 비닐이 흡입구 쪽에 빨려 붙지 않게 위에 지지대 같은 걸 대고요. 전체를 붙이려면 회색 테이프가 필요하고, 아래쪽을 막으려면 양말 같은 걸 넣어야 합니다.

quotes.speaker: Joe Kerwin (CAPCOM)
quotes.words_en: Okay. I think the equipment you'll need will be two Command Module lithium hydroxide canisters, a roll of the gray tape, the two LCGs, because we're going to use the bags from the LCGs, and one - one LM cue card - one of those cardboard cue cards...
quotes.context: GET 090:09:17. Start of the step-by-step build read-up (construction 090:22-091:10). LCG = liquid cooling garment, whose plastic bag is used. AFJ: no photos or film exist of the actual construction.
quotes.korean: 필요한 장비는 사령선 수산화리튬 통 두 개, 회색 테이프 한 롤, LCG 두 벌(LCG 포장 비닐을 쓸 겁니다), 그리고 착륙선 큐 카드, 그 판지로 된 카드 한 장입니다.

quotes.speaker: Jack Swigert (CMP) / Joe Kerwin (CAPCOM)
quotes.words_en: Swigert: Okay. Our do-it-yourself lithium hydroxide canister change is complete. ... / Kerwin: ...Jack. I concur. I think it'll work, too.
quotes.context: GET 091:10:26 / 091:10:53 (15 Apr about 08:23 CST). First mailbox finished. AFJ prints a typo 'do-it-yow'self' and Kerwin's 'Ok my, Jack'; AIRT has 'do-it-yourself'.
quotes.korean: 스위거트: 좋아요. 우리 손으로 만든 수산화리튬 통 교체 작업이 끝났습니다. / 커윈: 동의합니다. 저도 작동할 거라고 봅니다.

quotes.speaker: Joe Kerwin (CAPCOM) / Fred Haise
quotes.words_en: Kerwin: We are reading 0.2 on our CO2 sets here, and we're all delighted. It seems to be working fine. / Haise: Boy, that is great.
quotes.context: GET 094:33:21 / 094:33:31. CO2 partial pressure (mmHg) after switching to the CM canisters. AIRT has 'on our CO2 sensor'. Earlier, at 093:23:29, the ground read 6.6 while Haise's onboard gauge read 'about 12.5'.
quotes.korean: 커윈: 여기 CO2 수치가 0.2로 나옵니다. 다들 기뻐하고 있어요. 잘 작동하는 것 같습니다. / 헤이즈: 와, 정말 잘됐네요.

quotes.speaker: Jack Swigert (CMP) / Joe Kerwin (CAPCOM)
quotes.words_en: Swigert: Joe, did our sticky MOD on that ... those CO2 canisters work? / Kerwin: Jack, I think you asked if the canister MOD was working and the answer is, it sure as hell is.
quotes.korean: 스위거트: 조, 우리가 테이프로 붙인 그 CO2 통 개조, 효과 있었습니까? / 커윈: 잭, 통 개조가 효과 있냐고 물은 것 같은데, 대답은, 그럼요, 끝내주게 잘 되고 있습니다.

quotes.speaker: Fred Haise (LMP)
quotes.words_en: Okay. We went to 15 on the primary last night before I changed it...
quotes.context: GET 093:24:08. Highest onboard CO2 reading the crew mentions (mmHg) on the LM primary cartridge. Mission Report: the level 'was permitted to increase to an indicated 14.9 mm Hg'; the allowable limit was extended to 15 mmHg. The warning light trips at 7.6 mmHg.
quotes.korean: 어젯밤 1차 카트리지를 교체하기 전에 15까지 올라갔었습니다.

quotes.speaker: Jack Swigert (CMP), to Deke Slayton
quotes.words_en: I'll tell you, Deke, it's cold up in there. I don't know whether we'll be able to sleep up there tonight; it must be about 35 or 40 degrees. ... It's not uncomfortable at all in Aquarius, but it definitely is cold in Odyssey.
quotes.context: GET 102:10:42 and 102:11:12. Slayton asked 'How does it feel, Jack?' and answered 'Roger. That's just what I was worrying about.' Degrees are Fahrenheit (about 2-4 C); this is the crew's estimate for the CM cabin, not a reading.
quotes.korean: 솔직히 말해서, 디크, 위쪽은 추워요. 오늘 밤 거기서 잘 수 있을지 모르겠습니다. 35~40도(화씨, 섭씨 약 2~4도)는 될 겁니다. … 아쿠아리우스는 전혀 불편하지 않은데, 오디세이는 확실히 춥습니다.

quotes.speaker: Fred Haise (LMP)
quotes.words_en: They came ... both came down here rubbing their hands, shivering. It's pretty cool upstairs.
quotes.context: GET 112:12:16. Lovell and Swigert coming down from the CM into the LM. Lousma asks 'Are you keeping warm in the LM?' and Haise answers 'Yes. It's pretty reasonable down here.'
quotes.korean: 둘 다 손을 비비고 덜덜 떨면서 내려왔어요. 위층은 꽤 춥습니다.

quotes.speaker: Jim Lovell (CDR)
quotes.words_en: Joe, you might pass to our friends in Crew Systems that lunar boots make great footwarmers. ... Negative, Joe. It's just too cold in there.
quotes.context: GET 117:51:24 and 117:51:39 ('in there' = the CM; Kerwin had asked if anyone was sleeping in the CM). AIRT continues: 'I got Fred stashed over here to my left. He's asleep and Jack's sleeping on the engine cover.'
quotes.korean: 조, 승무원 장비 담당 친구들한테 전해 줘요. 달 착륙용 부츠가 훌륭한 발 난로라고. … 아니요, 조. 거긴 그냥 너무 추워요.

quotes.speaker: Jim Lovell (CDR)
quotes.words_en: Another note of interest to the crew systems people ... Tell them that they don't have to bother putting the refrigerator onboard. I just brought out some hot dogs, and they're practically frozen.
quotes.context: GET 118:56:50. Earlier, at 118:27:56, Kerwin asked: 'Have you guys put on any extra clothes to try and ward off the nip of Jack Frost?' Lovell: 'Well, the lunar boots and two pair of underwear...'
quotes.korean: 승무원 장비 담당자들께 하나 더 전해 주세요. 냉장고는 굳이 실을 필요 없다고요. 방금 핫도그를 꺼냈는데 거의 꽁꽁 얼어 있습니다.

quotes.speaker: Jack Swigert (CMP) / Vance Brand (CAPCOM)
quotes.words_en: Swigert: Okay; going back up into the refrigerator. / Brand: Hey, I thought it was the bedroom. / Swigert: Well, it's got a new name now, because it is about 30 degrees cooler.
quotes.context: GET 122:57:13-122:57:22. 'Refrigerator' = the powered-down CM Odyssey. 30 degrees Fahrenheit is about 17 C cooler. Brand: 'Roger. Returning to the deep freeze...' At 127:34:33 Swigert says: 'Yes, and we used to call the Command Module the bedroom and it's now the refrigerator.'
quotes.korean: 스위거트: 자, 다시 냉장고로 올라갑니다. / 브랜드: 어, 거긴 침실인 줄 알았는데요. / 스위거트: 이름이 바뀌었어요. 30도(화씨)쯤 더 추워졌거든요.

quotes.speaker: Vance Brand (CAPCOM) / Fred Haise
quotes.words_en: Haise: ...did you all get a readout on what the cabin temp was up there? / Brand: Yes, we're getting 45 to 46 degrees. / Haise: Now you see why we call it the refrigerator. / Brand: Yes, it's kind of a cold winter day up there, isn't it? Is it snowing in the Command Module yet?
quotes.context: GET 123:12:07-123:12:35. CM cabin telemetry 45-46 F = about 7-8 C. Haise then (123:12:59): '...every window in the Command Module is just covered with water droplets.'
quotes.korean: 헤이즈: 위쪽 선실 온도 수치 받았습니까? / 브랜드: 네, 45~46도(화씨, 섭씨 약 7~8도)로 나옵니다. / 헤이즈: 이제 왜 저희가 거길 냉장고라고 부르는지 아시겠죠. / 브랜드: 그렇네요, 거긴 추운 겨울날이군요. 사령선에 벌써 눈이 내립니까?

quotes.speaker: Vance Brand (CAPCOM)
quotes.words_en: That's correct. The plus X-axis pointing toward the Sun and perpendicular to the terminator of the Earth.
quotes.context: GET 103:51:07. Briefing for the manual MCC-5 burn, aimed by eye: Sun in the AOT and Earth's terminator in the COAS. Haise 103:50:21 describes the view: '...the cusp laying right on the Y-Y line.'
quotes.korean: 맞습니다. +X축이 태양을 향하고, 지구의 명암 경계선과 수직이 되게 하는 겁니다.

quotes.speaker: Fred Haise (LMP) / Jack Lousma (CAPCOM)
quotes.words_en: Haise: Ullage. ... / Lousma: Okay. Looks good. Nice work. / Haise: Let's hope it was.
quotes.context: GET 105:18:18 (ullage), burn about 14 s at 10% throttle; Lousma 105:19:46; Haise 105:19:51. Planned 7.8 fps, achieved 7.4, trimmed to 7.6 with RCS (AFJ).
quotes.korean: 헤이즈: 얼리지(점화 전 정렬 분사). … / 루스마: 좋아 보입니다. 잘했습니다. / 헤이즈: 그랬기를 바랍시다.

quotes.speaker: Jim Lovell (CDR)
quotes.words_en: And there's one whole side of that spacecraft missing.
quotes.context: GET 138:04:46 (17 Apr about 07:17 CST), about 2.5 min after SM jettison (Lovell 'SM Sep.' 138:02:06; PAO: separation at 138:02:08). Kerwin: 'Is that right?' (138:04:50). Identical in TEC (05 18 04 46), AFJ, AIRT and SP-350.
quotes.korean: 그리고 우주선 한쪽 면이 통째로 없어졌습니다.

quotes.speaker: Jim Lovell (CDR)
quotes.words_en: Right by the - Look out there, will you? Right by the high gain antenna, the whole panel is blown out, almost from the base to the engine.
quotes.korean: 바로 저기, 저기 좀 봐. 고이득 안테나 바로 옆에, 패널 전체가 날아갔어요. 거의 밑동부터 엔진까지.

quotes.speaker: Fred Haise (LMP)
quotes.words_en: That's the way it looks; unless that's just a dark brown streak. It's really a mess. ... Man, that's unbelievable!
quotes.context: GET 138:05:31 (about the SPS engine bell) and 138:09:09.
quotes.korean: 그렇게 보입니다. 그냥 짙은 갈색 줄무늬가 아니라면요. 완전히 엉망입니다. … 세상에, 믿을 수가 없네!

quotes.speaker: Jim Lovell (CDR) / Joe Kerwin (CAPCOM)
quotes.words_en: Lovell: Five. LM jettison. / Kerwin: Okay, copy that. Farewell, Aquarius, and we thank you.
quotes.context: GET 141:29:56 / 141:30:05 (17 Apr about 10:43 CST). The lifeboat is released 1 h 11 min before entry.
quotes.korean: 러벨: 5. 착륙선 분리. / 커윈: 알겠습니다, 확인. 잘 가라, 아쿠아리우스. 고마웠다.

quotes.speaker: Jack Swigert (CMP) / Joe Kerwin (CAPCOM)
quotes.words_en: Swigert: I know all of us here want to thank all you guys down there for the very fine job you did. / Lovell: That's affirm, Joe. / Kerwin: I'll tell you - We all had a good time doing it.
quotes.context: GET 142:22:28-142:22:38, about 18 min before Entry Interface.
quotes.korean: 스위거트: 여기 있는 저희 모두, 지상의 여러분이 해 주신 훌륭한 일에 감사드리고 싶습니다. / 러벨: 맞습니다, 조. / 커윈: 말하자면, 저희 모두 즐겁게 한 일입니다.

quotes.speaker: Joe Kerwin (CAPCOM)
quotes.words_en: Okay LOS is about a minute or a minute and a half; in entry attitude, we'd like Omni Charlie, and welcome home. Over.
quotes.context: GET 142:38:36. Last call before loss of signal and reentry blackout. Swigert: 'Thank you.' (142:38:45). Also Swigert 142:38:14: 'The mood fits the color.'
quotes.korean: 좋습니다. 신호 두절까지 1분에서 1분 반 남았습니다. 재진입 자세에서 옴니 찰리로 해 주십시오. 그리고, 집에 온 걸 환영합니다. 오버.

quotes.speaker: Joe Kerwin (CAPCOM) / Jack Swigert (CMP)
quotes.words_en: Kerwin: Odyssey, Houston standing by. Over. / Swigert: Okay, Joe. / Kerwin: Okay. We read you, Jack.
quotes.context: GET 142:46:03 / 142:46:08 / 142:46:12 (17 Apr 11:59 CST), first contact after blackout, relayed via the ARIA 4 aircraft. The PAO first said 'That was Jim Lovell responding with the Okay, Joe', then corrected: 'That was Command Module pilot Jack Swigert.' Predicted blackout end (final PAD) was EI+3:38, about 142:44:24, so voice came about 1 min 44 s after predicted LOS end. Kerwin next: 'We're looking at the weather on TV and it looks just as advertised; real good.'
quotes.korean: 커윈: 오디세이, 휴스턴 대기 중. 오버. / 스위거트: 오케이, 조. / 커윈: 좋아요, 들립니다, 잭.

quotes.speaker: Jack Swigert (CMP) / Joe Kerwin (CAPCOM)
quotes.words_en: Swigert: We got two good drogues. / Kerwin: Odyssey, Houston. We show you on the mains, it really looks great. ... Got you on television, babe.
quotes.context: GET 142:49:17 / 142:50:06 / 142:50:15. PAO: 'An extremely loud applause here in Mission Control.' Splashdown at 142:54:41 GET = 17 Apr 1970 12:07:41 CST (18:07:41 UTC), 21°38'24"S 165°21'42"W, about 1 mile from target (Mission Report); SP-350: less than four miles from USS Iwo Jima.
quotes.korean: 스위거트: 드로그 낙하산 두 개 정상. / 커윈: 오디세이, 휴스턴. 주 낙하산이 펴진 게 보입니다. 정말 멋져요. … TV로 보고 있어요, 친구.

quotes.speaker: Recovery helicopter 'Photo 1'
quotes.words_en: Photo-1. Splashdown at this time. The three chutes are displaced. They're in the water.
quotes.context: GET 142:54:56 on the recovery loop. Earlier, at 142:54:44: 'Photo 1's on station. Photo 1 observes splashdown at this time.'
quotes.korean: 포토 1. 지금 착수. 낙하산 세 개가 벗겨져 물 위에 있다.

quotes.speaker: FILM LINE (Tom Hanks as Lovell, 'Apollo 13', 1995) - NOT a mission quote
quotes.words_en: Houston, we have a problem.
quotes.context: MISQUOTE. The real words (055:55:35) are 'Houston, we've had a problem.' Screenwriter William Broyles Jr. said the past tense 'wasn't as dramatic' (Washington Post, 13 Apr 2017). The misquote predates the film: a 1974 TV drama was titled 'Houston, We've Got a Problem'. Lovell himself slipped into present tense in his 1999 JSC oral history ('And I say, Houston, we have a problem. We have a main B bus undervolt.'), so retellings by the crew are not a source for the exact words. Use 'we've had' on screen.
reported_by: Wikipedia 'Houston, we have a problem' (citing Washington Post 2017)
quotes.korean: (영화 대사, 실제 아님) 휴스턴, 문제가 있다.

quotes.speaker: FILM LINE (Ed Harris as Gene Kranz, 1995) - never said during the mission
quotes.words_en: Failure is not an option.
quotes.context: Invented for the 1995 film. FIDO Jerry Bostick told the screenwriters (Al Reinert, Bill Broyles): 'No, when bad things happened, we just calmly laid out all the options, and failure was not one of them.' Broyles then said it would be the film's tagline. Kranz later used it as the title of his 2000 memoir. It does not appear in the air-to-ground or FD-loop transcripts. The real Kranz line is 'Let's solve the problem, but let's not make it any worse by guessing' (056:10:46).
reported_by: Wikipedia 'Failure is not an option' (citing SpaceActs.com Bostick account)
Universe Today, '13 MORE Things That Saved Apollo 13, Epilogue'
quotes.korean: (영화 대사, 실제 아님) 실패는 선택지가 아니다.

quotes.speaker: FILM LINE (Tom Hanks as Lovell, 1995) - NOT a mission quote
quotes.words_en: Hello, Houston. This is Odyssey. It's good to see you again.
quotes.context: Film dialogue after the blackout. The real first post-blackout exchange is Kerwin 'Odyssey, Houston standing by. Over.' / Swigert 'Okay, Joe.' (142:46:03-08), spoken by Swigert, not Lovell.
quotes.korean: (영화 대사, 실제 아님) 휴스턴, 여기는 오디세이. 다시 보게 되어 반갑습니다.

quotes.speaker: FILM LINES (1995) - not in transcripts
quotes.words_en: 'We just put Sir Isaac Newton in the driver's seat.' / 'Let's work the problem, people. Let's not make things any worse by guessing.' / 'We just lost the moon.'
quotes.context: Newton line: the real line is Lovell 080:18:49 'We're now in the hands of tracking.' 'Work the problem': adapted from Kranz's real FD-loop line at 056:10:46. 'We just lost the moon': no transcript counterpart.
quotes.korean: (영화 대사, 실제 아님) '방금 아이작 뉴턴 경에게 운전대를 넘겼다' / '자, 문제를 풀자. 추측으로 상황을 더 나쁘게 만들지 말자' / '우린 방금 달을 잃었다'

quotes.speaker: Lovell / Haise - 1970 Technical Crew Debrief (postflight)
quotes.words_en: Lovell: There was a dull but definite bang - not much of a vibration, though. ... Haise: I felt just a slight shudder.
quotes.context: Postflight technical debrief, April 1970 (quoted in AFJ). Lovell was in the lower equipment bay, Swigert in the left seat, Haise in the LM/tunnel.
quotes.korean: 러벨: 둔하지만 분명한 '쾅' 소리가 났습니다. 진동은 별로 없었고요. … 헤이즈: 저는 살짝 흔들리는 걸 느꼈을 뿐입니다.

quotes.speaker: Jim Lovell - 1970 Technical Crew Debrief, with Swigert
quotes.words_en: Lovell: Houston came through with a technique for using CM LiOH canisters in the LM, which worked probably as well as the basic system. We ended up with a complete primary LiOH canister that we didn't use. ... It's like putting up the antenna in a liferaft. Does it work? Maybe it'll keep you busy for a while. / Swigert: I felt we had an unlimited supply of LiOH canisters.
quotes.context: A nuance for the CO2 segment: in hindsight the crew said the margin was larger than feared. The Mission Report, however, states 'there were insufficient lithium hydroxide cartridges in the lunar module to support the abort mission.' Avoid saying the mailbox alone saved them from certain death.
quotes.korean: 러벨: 휴스턴이 사령선 수산화리튬 통을 착륙선에서 쓰는 방법을 찾아냈고, 아마 원래 시스템만큼 잘 작동했을 겁니다. 결국 1차 통 하나는 통째로 안 쓰고 남았습니다. … 구명뗏목에서 안테나를 세우는 것과 비슷하죠. 효과가 있냐고요? 적어도 한동안 바쁘게는 해 주죠. / 스위거트: 저는 수산화리튬 통이 무한정 있다고 느꼈습니다.

quotes.speaker: Jim Lovell - 'Houston, We've Had a Problem', NASA SP-350 (1975)
quotes.words_en: Nine minutes later the roof fell in; rather, oxygen tank No. 2 blew up, causing No. 1 tank also to fail. We came to the slow conclusion that our normal supply of electricity, light, and water was lost, and we were about 200,000 miles from Earth.
quotes.context: Lovell's own account in Apollo Expeditions to the Moon, ch.13 ('9 minutes' after his TV sign-off at 055:46). Same text: 'The time was 2108 hours on April 13.'
quotes.korean: 9분 뒤, 하늘이 무너졌습니다. 정확히는 2번 산소 탱크가 폭발했고, 그 때문에 1번 탱크도 고장 났죠. 우리는 서서히 깨달았습니다. 평소의 전기와 빛과 물 공급이 끊겼고, 우리는 지구에서 약 20만 마일 떨어져 있다는 것을.

quotes.speaker: Jim Lovell - NASA SP-350 (1975)
quotes.words_en: We were as cold as frogs in a frozen pool, especially Jack Swigert, who got his feet wet and didn't have lunar overshoes. It wasn't simply that the temperature dropped to 38 F: the sight of perspiring walls and wet windows made it seem even colder.
quotes.context: Lovell's later account of the cold (38 F = 3.3 C; see the disputed temperatures in notes).
quotes.korean: 우리는 언 연못 속 개구리처럼 추웠습니다. 특히 발이 젖었는데 달 덧신도 없던 잭 스위거트가 그랬죠. 단지 기온이 화씨 38도(섭씨 약 3도)로 떨어져서만은 아니었습니다. 땀처럼 맺힌 벽과 젖은 창문을 보니 더 춥게 느껴졌습니다.

quotes.speaker: Fred Haise - JSC Oral History, 23 March 1999
quotes.words_en: My emotions at that time went to just a sick feeling in the pit of my stomach, because I knew by Mission Rules, without reference, that that meant the cancellation of the lunar mission.
quotes.context: Haise on seeing the O2 tank gauges at the bottom right after the bang. Later in the same interview: 'Within probably the first minute to 2 minutes, I knew we had lost the mission.'
reported_by: NASA JSC Oral History Project, Haise 23 Mar 1999 (nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/haisefw-3-23-99.pdf, pp.12-31 to 12-32)
quotes.korean: 그 순간 제 감정은, 그저 속이 메스꺼워지는 느낌이었습니다. 규정집을 볼 필요도 없이, 그건 달 착륙 임무가 취소된다는 뜻이라는 걸 알았거든요.

quotes.speaker: Fred Haise - JSC Oral History, 23 March 1999
quotes.words_en: There was no temperature meter in the lunar module, but I would suspect it's 40—35 to 40 degrees [Fahrenheit], somewhere in that range, because it froze the water tanks in the command and service module. So I suspect with the little equipment we were running, we were a little warmer than freezing but not a lot.
quotes.context: Haise on the cold in the LM ([Fahrenheit] is the transcript editor's insertion). He also says: 'We did put on all our—all—every pair of underwear we had in the vehicle.'
reported_by: NASA JSC Oral History Project, Haise 23 Mar 1999, p.12-36
quotes.korean: 착륙선엔 온도계가 없었지만, 제 짐작엔 화씨 35~40도(섭씨 약 2~4도) 정도였을 겁니다. 사령·기계선의 물탱크가 얼었으니까요. 돌리던 장비가 얼마 없었으니, 어는점보다 조금 따뜻했지만 그리 많이는 아니었을 겁니다.

quotes.speaker: Jim Lovell - JSC Oral History, 25 May 1999
quotes.words_en: And I'm coming back down through the tunnel, and suddenly there's a hiss-bang! And the spacecraft rocks back and forth.
quotes.context: Lovell's 1999 recollection of the explosion. Note the slight difference from the 1970 debrief ('dull but definite bang - not much of a vibration').
reported_by: NASA JSC Oral History Project, Lovell 25 May 1999 (nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/lovellja-5-25-99.pdf)
quotes.korean: 터널을 지나 내려오는데, 갑자기 '쉭-쾅!' 하더니 우주선이 앞뒤로 흔들렸습니다.

quotes.speaker: Jim Lovell - JSC Oral History, 25 May 1999
quotes.words_en: It didn't take much intelligence on my part to realize that the gas escaping from the rear end and the needle on my second and last tank were one and the same, and very shortly we would be out of oxygen.
quotes.context: On the venting observation.
reported_by: NASA JSC Oral History Project, Lovell 25 May 1999
quotes.korean: 뒤쪽에서 새어 나가는 가스와, 두 번째이자 마지막 탱크의 바늘이 같은 이야기라는 걸 깨닫는 데 대단한 머리가 필요하진 않았습니다. 곧 산소가 바닥날 거라는 거였죠.

quotes.speaker: Jim Lovell - JSC Oral History, 25 May 1999
quotes.words_en: Because the lunar module was only built to last 45 hours! Only built to support two people! And, you know, here we are: 200,000 miles from Earth and 90 hours from Earth.
quotes.context: On using the LM as a lifeboat (designed for 2 men, ~45 hours).
reported_by: NASA JSC Oral History Project, Lovell 25 May 1999
quotes.korean: 착륙선은 45시간만 버티도록 만들어졌으니까요! 두 사람만 태우도록요! 그런데 우리는 지구에서 20만 마일, 90시간 떨어진 곳에 있었습니다.

quotes.speaker: Jim Lovell - JSC Oral History, 25 May 1999
quotes.words_en: The thought crossed our mind that we were in deep trouble. But we never dwelled on it.
quotes.context: Answer to whether they feared never coming back.
reported_by: NASA JSC Oral History Project, Lovell 25 May 1999
quotes.korean: 우리가 아주 큰 곤경에 빠졌다는 생각이 스치긴 했습니다. 하지만 거기에 매달리지는 않았습니다.

quotes.notes:
PRIMARY SOURCES (all fetched and read; local copies under /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-aireels/82e206d8-83ed-5019-be3d-65c96a1bf62c/scratchpad/a13q/)
- AFJ = Apollo 13 Flight Journal, corrected transcript and commentary (Woods/Kemppanen/O'Brien/Turhanov/Waugh, updated 2026-02-22). The old history.nasa.gov/afj and nasa.gov/history/afj URLs now redirect to a landing page; the live site is https://apollojournals.org/afj/ap13fj/ (pages 07..30). Combined text: a13q/afj_all.txt.
- TEC = NASA 'Apollo 13 Technical Air-to-Ground Voice Transcription' (MSC, 1970), https://apollojournals.org/alsj/a13/AS13_TEC.PDF (21 MB, 765 pp). The JSC portal URL redirects. Timestamps are DD HH MM SS. Speaker labels are sometimes wrong (the 55:55:19-20 call is labeled LMP/CDR). Text: a13q/tec/tec.txt.
- AIRT = Apollo 13 in Real Time (Ben Feist), https://apolloinrealtime.org/13/indexes/utteranceData.csv, format GET|speaker|text|type (T crew, C CAPCOM, F MOCR flight loop, P PAO). FD-loop transcripts cover only 055-062 h. Local: a13q/utteranceData.csv.
- Mission Report MSC-02680 and Review Board report: apollojournals.org/afj/ap13fj/pdf/ (local a13q/docs/*.txt).
- Lovell SP-350 ch.13: the nasa.gov copy redirects to NTRS; I used the mirror apolloexplorer.co.uk/books/sp-350/ch-13-1..5.html.
- JSC Oral Histories: Haise 23 Mar 1999 (nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/haisefw-3-23-99.pdf) and Lovell 25 May 1999 (nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/08/lovellja-5-25-99.pdf). These are transcripts only, not audio.

TIME CONVERSION: GET 0 = range zero 19:13:00 GMT 11 Apr 1970 = 13:13 CST (Mission Report). No GET clock update on Apollo 13 (that happened on Apollo 14).
- O2 tank 2 failure 55:54:53 (telemetry loss 55:54:53.555, RB) = 13 Apr 21:07:53 CST = 14 Apr 03:07:53 UTC = 14 Apr 12:07:53 KST. RB: 'approximately 55:55 g.e.t. (10:08 p.m.e.s.t.)'. Lovell SP-350: 'The time was 2108 hours on April 13.'
- First call 55:55:19-20 = 21:08:19 CST. Venting call 56:09:07. Crew into the LM about 57:41. PC+2 ignition about 79:27:38 = 14 Apr 20:40 CST. First mailbox done 91:10 = 15 Apr 08:23 CST. SM jettison 138:02:06-08. LM jettison 141:30:00. 'Okay, Joe' 142:46:08 = 17 Apr 11:59 CST. Splashdown 142:54:41 = 17 Apr 12:07:41 CST = 18:07:41 UTC = 18 Apr 03:07:41 KST.

AUDIO POINTERS (US-government public domain; for the audio agent)
- AFJ serves direct MP3s at apollojournals.org/afj/ap13fj/audio/a13_HHHMMSS.mp3, but only up to about 057:08. Clips:
  - a13_0555519.mp3 (379 s; starts about 055:54:52). Swigert 'Okay... we've had a problem here' 26.5-28.3 s. Lousma 'This is Houston. Say again, please.' 35.6-36.9 s. Lovell 'Houston, we've had a problem.' 42.1-43.2 s and '...Main B Bus Undervolt.' 46.7-47.7 s. Lousma 'Roger, Main B undervolt' 49.7-50.4 s.
  - a13_0560317.mp3 (407 s; starts about 056:03:16). O2-zero line 341-347 s; venting 354-364 s; 'Roger, we copy your venting' 365.6-366.5 s; 'gas of some sort' about 372-373 s.
  - Offsets are from faster-whisper word timestamps; verify by ear.
- Later events (mailbox, cold, SM jettison, entry) have no AFJ MP3. AIRT plays air-to-ground through YouTube embeds, which are blocked here. Its MOCR loop audio is at https://media.apolloinrealtime.org/A13/MOCR_audio/DA13_{tape}_{x}_16khz_mp3_16/DA13_{tape}_{x}_CH{n}.mp3, with the tape mapping in MOCR_audio/tape_activity/*.json. FD loop = channel 50.

DISPUTED NUMBERS (best primary source first)
1. Distance at the explosion: AFJ commentary '178,000 nautical miles' (about 329,700 km); PAO at 056:12 '178,643 nautical miles' (330,847 km); Lovell SP-350 and 1999 OH 'about 200,000 miles' (statute, about 322,000 km). The interviewer's '240,000' is wrong. Neither the RB nor the Mission Report gives a figure. Recommend 'about 330,000 km' (약 33만 km), or '약 32만 km' if quoting Lovell.
2. Cabin temperature (all °F):
  - Mission Report: CM cabin 'decreased to approximately 43 °F' (6 °C); LM cabin 'typically between 54° and 60 °F' (12-16 °C), though 'the lunar module also cooled down to an extent where sleep was not possible for approximately the last 16 hours'.
  - Air-to-ground: Brand at 123:12:20, CM telemetry 45-46 °F (7-8 °C). Swigert's estimate at 102:10:42: '35 or 40'.
  - PAO at about 134:56: LM cabin about 54 °F before power-up.
  - Lovell SP-350: 38 °F (3.3 °C). Haise OH: '35 to 40', 'a little warmer than freezing' (no LM thermometer).
  - Recommend '영상 3~8도, 어는점 바로 위' and avoid 'below freezing'.
3. CO2 partial pressure (mmHg):
  - Warning light at 7.6. The limit was extended to 15 (Mission Report sec. 9), and the level reached an indicated 14.9 (sec. 6.7). Haise: 'We went to 15 on the primary'.
  - At 093:23 the gauges disagreed (ground 6.6, onboard about 12.5).
  - After the CM-canister rig: 0.1-1.8 (Mission Report); Kerwin read 0.2.
  - Avoid 'lethal level' claims.
4. Reentry blackout:
  - Final entry PAD (PAO about 141:53): Entry Interface (EI) 142:40:46, blackout from EI+0:19 to EI+3:38, i.e. predicted end about 142:44:24.
  - First voice was 142:46:08, about 1 min 44 s after the predicted end, roughly 5 min after blackout began. Kerwin's first call came right after the PAO reported 'ARIA 4 aircraft has Acquisition Of Signal'.
  - AFJ: a 'longer than expected blackout' (shallow entry angle) is a favorite topic of speculation, but the original reports do not address it.
  - Popular claims such as '6 minutes' or '87 s longer' have no primary source. Safer wording: '예상보다 1분 넘게 응답이 없었다'.
5. Burns:
  - Free-return MCC-4: about 61:30 GET, 38 fps (RB).
  - PC+2: about 79:28, 263.4 s burn (RB).
  - Manual MCC-5 (Earth terminator plus Sun in the AOT): 105:18, about 14 s at 10% throttle, 7.4 fps achieved, trimmed to 7.6 (AFJ).
6. LM as a lifeboat: Lovell (1999 OH) says it was 'only built to last 45 hours' for 'two people'. The task brief's '~2 days' is fine.

MOVIE/MISQUOTE FLAGS (rows marked disputed)
- 'Houston, we have a problem': the real tense is 'we've had'. Even Lovell misquotes it in the 1999 OH.
- 'Failure is not an option': coined via Jerry Bostick's interview with the screenwriters; title of Kranz's 2000 book; in no mission transcript.
- 'Hello Houston, this is Odyssey, it's good to see you again': film. The real line is Swigert's 'Okay, Joe.'
- 'Sir Isaac Newton in the driver's seat': film. The real line is 'We're now in the hands of tracking.'
- 'Work the problem, people': film paraphrase of Kranz's real line.
- 'We just lost the moon': film.
- AFJ warns that documentaries show venting footage that is really a water dump from another flight. Do not present any such footage as real.

RECOMMENDATIONS
- For the hook, use Lovell's clean and undisputed 055:55:35 clip (about 5.7 s): 'Houston, we've had a problem. We've had a Main B Bus Undervolt.' Swigert's first call is shorter (about 2 s) but its wording is disputed ('I believe' in TEC/AIRT, absent in AFJ). If you use it, subtitle 'Okay, Houston... we've had a problem here.'
- Korean '문제가 생겼습니다' fits the present perfect.
- Attribute all MOCR-loop lines (Kranz, Lunney, Merritt) as Mission Control internal loop, not air-to-ground.
- Haise's onboard remarks such as 'There she goes, gang. The Moon.' were picked up on VOX.
- I found no notable verbatim lines for Flight Directors Windler or Griffin. AIRT's FD-loop transcripts cover only 055-062 h, which is Kranz's and Lunney's shifts.

media.notes:
I found and downloaded real NASA audio for all seven key moments. There are 12 WAV files (mono, 16-bit, 44.1 or 48 kHz, 43 MB in total) in /home/user/aireels/assets/apollo13_media/. The folder is gitignored (git status shows nothing). All final audio comes from the NASA JSC Houston Audio Control Room digitization on the Internet Archive (item Apollo13Audio, Public Domain Mark), not from any film or documentary. Each file name gives the start GET and the source tape and track. Clip times are seconds within each local file. I transcribed only short windows with faster-whisper medium (int8, 2 CPU threads, numpy input). words_en follows the NASA / Apollo in Real Time transcript wording wherever Whisper misheard; those cases are marked in the clip notes. Whisper also hallucinates 'CAPCOM' and 'SC' labels at segment starts, so ignore them.

What was available and how it is served:
1) Internet Archive item Apollo13Audio. It holds 7-track 'Historical MC' tapes 405-429 (each about 6.5 h, WAV, FLAC and MP3), plus Flight Director loop tapes 787-790 and 795, EECOM-Loop-During-Accident and Apollo-13-Problem (a 98-min NASA compilation with the silences removed). The WAVs are uncompressed PCM with the audio data starting at byte 1024, so I fetched only the seconds I needed with HTTP range requests. The tape-start times in the item's metadata PDF are rough (418 is labelled 79:10 but actually starts about 77:10), so I calibrated each tape against the transcript or against the MOCR audio below. Tracks 1, 3 and 5 carry the air-to-ground loop; track 3 also carries PAO commentary. Tape 428 has no track 5.
2) apolloinrealtime.org/13 (Ben Feist's project). Its main air-to-ground audio is served through YouTube, which is blocked here, so I did not test it. Its Mission Control (MOCR) loop audio is downloadable as constant-bitrate MP3 per channel (8 kHz audio at 16 kbps, 2000 bytes/s). The URL pattern is media.apolloinrealtime.org/A13/MOCR_audio/DA13_<tape>_<HR1L|HR1U|HR2..>_16khz_mp3_16/DA13_<tape>_<HR>_CH<n>.mp3, and the tape start GETs are in /13/MOCRviz/data/tape_ranges.csv. The byte offset is (GET minus tape start) x 2000. Channels 14 and 15 (CAPCOM) contain the air-to-ground mixed with flight-loop chatter. The site itself is licensed CC BY-NC-SA, so I used these files only to line up times (envelope cross-correlation) and as fallbacks. None of the delivered files come from them.
3) Apollo-13-Problem.ogg from the same Archive item: clean 48 kHz air-to-ground plus PAO from 55:50 GET onward, with the silences removed. The problem exchange is at 85.1-102.6 s and the venting line at 385.2-402.0 s. It is a usable alternate but was not saved to assets.
4) Not used: the Archive item 'Apollo-13-problemLastPart' (a community re-edit that was reversed and re-pitched) and anything with music.

Recommended picks:
- Swigert, 01 14.45-17.15
- Lovell, 01 29.9-36.85
- Lovell venting, 02 17.3-21.1 and 25.15-28.15
- Lousma lifeboat, 03 10.0-16.0
- Haise 'Didn't think I'd be back this soon', 04 30.9-35.5
- Brand mailbox, 05 23.3-28.7
- Swigert 'canister change is complete', 07 9.0-14.95 (heavy hiss)
- Swigert 'too cold to sleep', 08 26.25-30.75
- Lovell 'one whole side... missing', 09 20.15-23.15
- Reentry, 10 10.0-16.15
- Main chutes, 11 8.6-12.2
- Splashdown, 12 16.55-20.1

On-screen attribution: 'NASA 교신 음성 (Apollo 13, 1970) · 퍼블릭 도메인 · NASA JSC/Internet Archive'.

Audio quality: Quindar beeps (about 250 ms at 2525 Hz on keying and 2475 Hz on release) bracket CAPCOM lines; the detected times are in the clip notes. Files 01-03, 08 and 10-12 are clean (noise floor -44 to -49 dB). File 04 has some hiss and file 05 a little more. Files 06 and 07 have heavy hiss, because the LM downlink was weak at low power ('our downlink is pretty noisy', as Kerwin said at the time).

Disputed points and primary sources:
(a) Swigert's first call. The 1970 NASA transcript has 'Okay, Houston, we've had a problem here', and all 5 Whisper passes hear 'we've had'. The Apollo Flight Journal and Apollo in Real Time reading is 'Okay, Houston - [Lovell: Houston] - I believe we've had a problem here.' Lovell's 'Houston, we've had a problem. We've had a Main B Bus Undervolt.' (55:55:35) is undisputed.
(b) 'Houston, we have a problem' is the 1995 film's misquote.
(c) 'Failure is not an option' was never said on any mission loop. It is a 1995 film line, credited to the screenwriters after an interview with flight controller Jerry Bostick, and later the title of Kranz's 2000 book.
(d) Explosion time: 55:54:53.5 GET, 13 Apr 1970 about 21:08 CST, according to the Review Board report. I did not re-read that report in this session.
(e) Distance at the explosion. The PAO on the tapes said 177,861 nmi (329,399 km) at 55:46:34 GET and 178,643 nmi at about 56:12 (heard on the NASA compilation). That puts the explosion at about 330,000 km, roughly 205,000 statute miles. The popular '200,000 miles / 320,000 km' is a rounded figure. I suggest '약 33만 km'.
(f) Cold. Swigert at 102:10:42 GET estimated the CM at 'about 35 or 40 degrees' (°F, about 2-4 °C). The PAO at 140:21 said the CM read 38 °F (about 3 °C). The LM was about 51-54 °F according to the PAO at 124:15 and 133:14. I did not check the Mission Report figure.
(g) CO2, from the air-to-ground loop. At 82:53:35 Lousma said 11.3 mm Hg with a 'medical go up to 15 millimeters'. At 85:22 it was about 15, and the crew swapped to the secondary cartridge (4.5 afterwards). At 93:23 Haise read about 12.5 onboard while the ground read 6.6, a gauge discrepancy, and they then moved to the CM canisters. Brand first described the adapter at 80:22. Kerwin read up the build procedure from 90:09, and Swigert reported it complete at 91:10:26.
(h) Blackout. From the PAO and the transcript: the PAO at 142:44:19 said less than 10 s were left of the predicted blackout. ARIA 4 acquired the signal at about 142:45:51, and Swigert's 'Okay, Joe' came at 142:46:08. That makes contact about 1.5-2 minutes later than predicted. The often-quoted '6 minutes' and '87 s longer' are not verified.
(i) Splashdown: 142:54:41 GET, 17 Apr 1970 12:07:41 CST, south Pacific near USS Iwo Jima. All three crew survived.

Not obtained: Lovell's reply to the post-splashdown crew-condition call (142:59:07, 'We're in good shape...'). It is in the downloaded tape-428 portion but too unclear to transcribe reliably.

draft.caption_ko:
[실화] 지구에서 약 33만 km, 산소 탱크가 터진 아폴로 13호
※ 실제 NASA 교신 음성(1970)이 포함되어 있습니다.

1970년 4월 13일 밤 9시 7분(휴스턴 시각, 한국 시각 14일 낮 12시 7분), 달로 가던 아폴로 13호의 기계선에서 2번 산소 탱크가 터졌습니다. 탱크 속 산소를 휘젓는 팬을 켠 지 약 1분 반 뒤였습니다. 승무원은 선장 짐 러벨, 사령선 조종사 잭 스와이거트, 착륙선 조종사 프레드 헤이즈.

1번 탱크의 산소까지 새면서 사령선 '오디세이'의 연료전지가 모두 멈췄습니다. 세 사람은 재진입용 배터리를 아끼려 사령선을 끄고, 두 사람이 약 45시간 쓰도록 만든 착륙선 '아쿠아리우스'에서 약 84시간을 버텼습니다. 물은 1인당 하루 약 180mL였습니다(러벨의 회고).

착륙선의 이산화탄소 흡수통은 귀환까지 모자랐고, 사령선 흡수통은 모양이 맞지 않았습니다. 휴스턴의 엔지니어들이 비닐봉지·판지·덕트 테이프·우주복 호스로 만든 어댑터('우편함')를 지상에서 먼저 만들어 시험했고, 교신으로 단계별로 불러 줬습니다.

이미 자동 귀환 궤도를 벗어나 있었기 때문에, 착륙선 엔진으로 궤도를 되찾고 달 뒤편을 돈 뒤 다시 점화해 귀환을 앞당겼습니다. 이후 두 번은 창밖 지구를 기준으로 손으로 자세를 잡아 궤도를 고쳤습니다. 4월 17일(휴스턴 시각) 남태평양에 착수했고, 폭발 약 87시간 만에 세 사람 모두 살아 돌아왔습니다.

출처마다 다른 숫자와 기록
· 폭발 지점: NASA 발표 약 17만 8천 해리(약 33만 km). '20만 마일(약 32만 km)'은 어림수입니다.
· 추위: 사령선 약 6°C(임무 보고서), 승무원 추정 2~4°C. 지내던 착륙선은 대체로 11~16°C. 영하였다는 기록은 없습니다.
· 이산화탄소: 경고 기준 7.6 mmHg를 의료진이 15로 올렸고, 최고 14.9였습니다. 임무 보고서상 건강 이상은 없었습니다.
· 통신 두절: 예측은 약 3분 19초, 첫 음성은 예측보다 약 1분 44초 늦었습니다. 늦어진 이유는 공식 보고서에 없습니다.
· 첫 호출 "Okay, Houston… we've had a problem here"는 기록마다 화자와 문구가 조금 다릅니다. 영상 속 음성은 이견이 없는 러벨의 두 번째 호출입니다.
· "Houston, we have a problem"과 "Failure is not an option"은 1995년 영화 대사로, 실제 교신에는 없습니다.

원인(NASA 조사위원회, 1970): 발사 전 지상 작업에서 28V용 온도 스위치가 65V 전원에 녹아붙어 탱크 속 전선 피복이 손상됐고, 비행 중 합선으로 불이 나 탱크가 터졌습니다.

짐 러벨은 2025년, 잭 스와이거트는 1982년 세상을 떠났습니다. 프레드 헤이즈는 유일한 생존 승무원으로 알려져 있습니다(2026년 4월 보도 기준).

음성: NASA 아폴로 13호 교신 녹음(1970, 미국 정부 저작물·퍼블릭 도메인), NASA JSC 디지털화본(Internet Archive 'Apollo13Audio'). 대사는 NASA 녹취록, Apollo Flight Journal과 대조했습니다. 영화·다큐멘터리의 음성과 음악은 쓰지 않았습니다. 그림은 모두 직접 그린 일러스트이며 실제 인물의 얼굴은 그리지 않았습니다. 이 영상은 NASA와 무관합니다.
